canberra.title: Four sheep dead after sickening night of alleged animal cruelty
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article contains distressing content. Four sheep have died in what is alleged to have been a sickening and horrific...
canberra.content:
13 October 2026

Four sheep (not pictured) died after an alleged animal cruelty incident in Tuggeranong. Photo: Alfio Manciagli.

CONTENT WARNING: This article contains distressing content.

Four sheep have died in what is alleged to have been a sickening and horrific animal cruelty case in southern Canberra.

According to court documents obtained by Region after 18-year-old Memphis Auld applied for bail over the allegations, it appeared the sheep were shot with a gun and cut with a weapon by intruders on a rural property.

The documents say a woman had eight merino sheep which she used to train working cattle dogs as part of her business. The sheep were kept in paddocks on a rural property in the Tuggeranong region, which was owned by a farmer.

Over the night of 16-17 September 2026, intruders allegedly used an angle grinder to cut through a padlock on a gate at the property then ransacked its homestead.

In addition, the intruders allegedly mustered the sheep into a holding yard and began firing a .22 calibre gun at the animals, killing one and injuring others.

According to the documents, the woman arrived in the morning and found her sheep with horrific injuries. She also found a sword which had been stabbed into the ground in the yard.

Police were called and had to euthanise one of the sheep themselves as the severity of its injuries meant it would have been in extreme pain. A vet examined five of the remaining animals and found they had penetrating wounds, cuts, facial trauma, blood loss and swelling.

Other vets later said two of the sheep had significant injuries associated with gunshot trauma and needed to be euthanised.

This means the intruders were alleged to have killed one sheep on the night, then caused severe injuries to three others that resulted in them needing to be put down.

Police seized this knife from the Richardson home where they arrested 18-year-old Memphis Auld. Photo: ACT Policing.

The court documents allege that when the owner of the rural property returned home around 11 pm on 17 September, he saw a silver sedan parked at his front gate.

The sedan sped off when he approached. The owner drove after it, but he alleged the front passenger of the sedan leaned out the window and pointed a gun at him.

He lost the sedan in Chisholm.

Due to information from witnesses and CCTV, police began looking for a silver Kia Rio, which they tracked down to a residence in Bonython that was linked to a 27-year-old man. Region hasn’t named the man for the time being.

When police looked at CCTV from this residence, they allegedly saw the 27-year-old had been driving the car to and from the home several times over the night of 16-17 September.

He was allegedly filmed in the car with three others, including Mr Auld, over this time. Police allege at one stage Mr Auld left the home with a sawn-off .22 rifle hidden inside his pants.

The 27-year-old man was arrested for unrelated reasons in late September. When police looked at his phone, they allegedly found a photo of a man pointing a gun at sheep in a holding yard as well as another showing a sheep with what looked like blood on its face.

Police then raided Mr Auld’s home in Richardson last week.

He faced the ACT Magistrates Court on Friday (9 October) where he applied for bail. However, his application was refused and he was remanded in custody before his matter was adjourned to 27 October.

He has been charged with four counts of animal cruelty causing death by joint commission as well as single counts of animal cruelty causing injury by joint commission, burglary and possessing a prohibited firearm.

It was not immediately clear if pleas had been entered.

It is expected police will charge the 27-year-old man as well, while a 16-year-old has been arrested then released pending further investigation.

If you or someone you know needs help, you can contact Lifeline’s 24-hour crisis support line on 13 11 14.

canberra.title: Row erupts despite $10 million to keep Burrangiri respite aged care operating
canberra.snippet: The Albanese Government has come through with $10 million to keep the Burrangiri Aged Care Respite Centre in Rivett open, but it has been...
canberra.content:
Senator David Pocock speaking at a rally for Burrangiri respite aged care centre in Rivett last year. He says the funding should have delivered more beds. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

The Albanese Government has come through with $10 million to keep the Burrangiri Aged Care Respite Centre in Rivett open, but it has been accused of breaking an election promise to increase the number of respite beds in the ACT.

The government said the funding would deliver on a 2025 election commitment to ensure Burrangiri could continue to provide aged care respite services.

The commitment came after the ACT Government’s decision to close the Salvation Army-run Burrangiri sparked a storm of protest from families using the facility, backed by Independent MLA Fiona Carrick and Independent Senator David Pocock.

The ACT Government said the facility was no longer fit for purpose and needed refurbishment, but kept it open when the Commonwealth came to the party, extending the contract with the Salvation Army to mid-2027.

The ACT Government will receive $10 million through the Aged Care Capital Assistance Program (ACCAP) for infrastructure upgrades to fix work health and safety issues at the facility.

Works will begin in the second half of 2027 and be completed in 2028.

The Department of Health, Disability and Ageing will open an expression of interest process later this month to find providers who can deliver replacement respite services from July 2027.

The Commonwealth said it would also continue exploring options, including a proposal already received from Goodwin Aged Care, to meet the longer-term respite care needs of older Canberrans and their families as demand for services grows.

But Senator Pocock said spending the $10 million on upgrades rather than expanding Burrangiri would not deliver extra respite beds as promised.

He said a proposal from a local residential aged care provider that would have allowed safety upgrades to Burrangiri and an additional 18 respite beds appeared to have been overlooked.

Senator Pocock said about $2.7 million would be spent on essential fire safety upgrades at Burrangiri and a further $7.4 million in broader building improvement works, including to “refresh” the finishes on the building without adding to the respite bed capacity.

“Canberra has a shortage of respite beds, and we were promised additional beds at the last election. Now we see federal Labor walking away from that commitment 18 months later,” Senator Pocock said.

“We were promised more respite beds. It is so frustrating when there is a proposal from an aged care provider that would have allowed safety upgrades to Burrangiri and 18 more respite beds within the funding envelope.”

But federal Finance Minister and ACT senator Katy Gallagher said Senator Pocock was wrong; the commitment was to ensure Burrangiri could keep operating.

“That was what he originally called for as well, and that is what we’ve done,” she said.

“We have spent countless hours in meetings, including with Senator Pocock and Fiona Carrick, to try to work out the best way to keep Burrangiri open, to not reduce servicing in the ACT, to do what the carers and residents of Burrangiri want and, indeed, what the independents have been calling for.

“This does that. There is more work to do about the provision of respite care here in the ACT. We’re doing that work as well.”

Senator Gallagher said if there were capacity to provide extra beds, the government would have done so.

“The reality is, with all of the reports we’ve got, with the meetings that we’ve had, that money is required to ensure Burrangiri stays open, and we are looking at what we do to provide continuity of care for people who use Burrangiri when it closes for this refurbishment.

“And then, separately, we are looking at the broader issue of how do we build up enough aged care respite beds in the ACT? Because clearly that’s an area of pressure.”

ACT Minister for Health Infrastructure Rachel Stephen-Smith said the funding was a win-win for Canberrans.

“Burrangiri will be refurbished, while also recognising the need for expanded respite in a range of settings,” she said.

canberra.title: APSC offers public servants 9 per cent pay rise over three years
canberra.snippet: Commonwealth public servants have been offered a 9 per cent pay rise over three years, which some unionists say is nowhere near good enou...
canberra.content:
The Australian Public Service Commission has tabled a 9 per cent pay rise for public servants, but the CPSU isn’t impressed. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Commonwealth public servants have been offered a 9 per cent pay rise over three years, which some unionists say is nowhere near good enough.

The Australian Public Service Commission tabled the Federal Government’s proposed pay package as part of the APS-wide bargaining process.

The package includes guaranteed pay rises for eligible APS employees over the next three years and further measures to support greater consistency in pay across the APS.

The offer includes a 3.2 per cent rise for APS employees from next March, then 3 per cent from March 2028, and 2.8 per cent in March 2029.

Some workers in agencies with lower pay grades will get further salary increases up to 0.5 per cent each of the three years (or a total of up to 1.5 per cent) to help close the pay gap between departments.

A new minimum pay point increase of 3 per cent is included for eligible employees progressing through their salary range where their existing advancement increase is lower than 3 per cent.

APS-wide conditions are also being negotiated, and include consistent flexible working arrangements, reduced qualifying periods for higher duties allowance, and stronger leave portability when joining the APS from another government employer.

APS chief negotiator Alison Stott said the proposal builds on the work from the previous bargaining round.

“This proposal delivers guaranteed pay rises while also increasing consistency in pay between agencies and creating more consistent salary advancement across the APS,” Ms Stott said.

“For eligible employees, the additional salary uplifts and advancement changes mean increases above the headline pay rise.

“We’re building on the work of the previous bargaining round to increase commonality across APS agencies.

“This measure will uplift at least one classification in 92 per cent of agencies.

“This pay is part of an overall package of conditions. These are preliminary positions within this package, not agreed outcomes.

“Bargaining is continuing and we will keep working with unions and individual bargaining representatives in good faith.”

She said the proposed pay rises provide certainty about salary increases over the next three years and are above the 2.5 per cent CPI per annum inflation rate projected in the 2026–27 Budget over a similar period.

But the Community and Public Sector Union says the offer falls short of its claim.

The CPSU’s membership endorsed claims of 5 per cent each year or CPI, whichever is higher.

The union’s negotiating team took that pay claim to the bargaining table.

It is now asking its members to decide whether the government’s offer is good enough for federal public sector employees.

CPSU national secretary Rebecca Fawcett said it would be up to members to vote whether to accept the offer.

“CPSU members have been clear from the beginning of these negotiations – they want to see pay that keeps up with the cost of living, which recognises the essential work they do every day,” Ms Fawcett said.

“The APS-wide pay offer that has been tabled (Tuesday 13 October) falls short of what our members asked for, and what public sector workers deserve.

“This is now in our members’ hands. They will decide whether it is good enough, and the union will continue to fight for a pay offer that respects these vital workers, and the important services they deliver to the community.”

The union has launched a poll giving CPSU members the opportunity to voice their opinions on the pay offer.

All public sector workers are encouraged to have their say, but only CPSU members can participate in the CPSU’s poll on the pay offer.

Last week, more than 15,000 workers voiced their concerns about APSC proposals that would take members’ rights backwards, affecting flex time, Christmas closedown, annual leave and working-hours provisions.

The union expects public sector workers to send an even stronger message to the government on pay.

The CPSU says it was “ready and willing” to bargain since April, but the APSC only started negotiations in July.

More than 39,000 employees participated in the 2026 APS Employment Conditions Survey, with 79 per cent identifying base salary as a condition that matters most when deciding whether to join or remain in the APS.

The APS-wide bargaining process will continue until agreement is reached.

canberra.title: Female care sector employees to receive fairer pay after Fair Work Commission findings
canberra.snippet: More than 460,000 female health, disability and community services workers will receive fairer pay and work conditions following findings...
canberra.content:
Services Minister Katy Gallagher said the FWC findings and payments were a significant step towards ensuring women were properly recognised and rewarded for their contribution to the care sector. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

More than 460,000 female health, disability and community services workers will receive fairer pay and work conditions following findings by the Fair Work Commission.

The FWC findings recognised that female employees’ work in the care sector has been undervalued because of gender-based assumptions. As a result, the Federal Government has undertaken to invest $630 million to deliver fairer pay.

The FWC’s decision was handed down in September, and affects workers covered by the Social, Community, Home Care and Disability Services Industry Award 2010.

It followed submissions filed by the Australian Services Union (ASU), Australian Industry Group (Ai Group), and a number of individuals calling for pay rises to be brought forward after the FWC agreed in June to restructure the award. The ASU also took its case to Parliament in September to ask the government to support its case.

As a result, workers affected received an up-to 15 per cent wage rise from 1 October, with any residual increase to be paid from 1 October, 2027. The award’s various schedules will also be replaced with a new classification structure from 1 October, 2027.

The government said the FWC’s decisions to award pay rises to the care sector workforce were a direct result of its gender-equality reforms as part of the Fair Work Act. It said the investment would provide award-related wage changes for workers in more than 128,000 charities and not-for-profit organisations that delivered 92 government programs.

Services Minister Katy Gallagher said the gender pay gap could not be closed without confronting and addressing the historic undervaluation of work performed by women.

“Australia’s gender pay gap is at a record low, and this is another significant step towards ensuring women are properly recognised and rewarded for their contribution,” Senator Gallagher said.

“This move is also a clear signal that this workforce and the support they provide our community is important and valued.”

The government said health, disability and community service workers provided essential care and support to Australians at every stage of life, and they deserved fair pay that reflected their skills, expertise and the vital contribution they made to the community.

It said the funding would also support government-funded organisations that employed workers in other sectors affected by the award changes, including legal assistance workers, housing workers, youth workers, community development workers and First Nations health and community services workers.

Minister for Employment and Workplace Relations Amanda Rishworth said work performed in female-dominated industries had not been properly recognised or valued for too long.

“The government changed the law to put gender equality at the heart of the Fair Work Act because women deserve to be paid fairly for the work they do,” she said.

“This Fair Work Commission decision is helping to address decades of gender-based undervaluation and deliver better wages for workers in health, disability and community services.

“This is what closing the gender pay gap looks like in practice — recognising the value of women’s work contributions and helping Australian workers earn more.”

Health Minister Mark Butler added: “Health, disability and community workers provide critical services to help Australians in time of need, and they deserve to be paid fairly for their work.

“This investment will not only help retain existing workers, it will make this sector a more attractive career path to build a stronger workforce for the future.”

Minister for Social Services Tanya Plibersek said: “Behind every community service is a dedicated worker helping someone through one of the hardest moments of their life.

“Whether it’s supporting a woman escaping violence, helping a family facing homelessness, or making sure someone has a warm meal and somewhere to turn, these workers change lives every day.

“Fairer pay will support a stronger, more sustainable community sector and ensure Australians can continue to access the services they need when they need them most.”

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

canberra.title: Woman admits sexually abusing young boy over several months
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to child abuse. A woman has admitted sexually abusing a young teenage boy over several months and wi...
canberra.content:
13 October 2026

Jessica May Nakkan (right) leaves the ACT Courts on Tuesday with her solicitor, Himangi Ticku, after pleading guilty. Photo: Albert McKnight.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to child abuse.

A woman has admitted sexually abusing a young teenage boy over several months and will face court to be sentenced next year.

It has previously been alleged that Jessica May Nakkan was 29 when she sexually abused a boy, who was under 16, in 2025.

She was arrested that year, pleaded not guilty and was granted bail while the charges moved through the courts.

Then on Tuesday (13 October), the now-31-year-old faced the ACT Supreme Court and was arraigned on a new, single count of the persistent sexual abuse of a child.

“Guilty,” she softly said.

The prosecutor said the plea would be accepted in full satisfaction of the indictment, meaning her other charges will no longer proceed because of her guilty plea on this charge.

Through her plea, Nakkan admitted to sexually abusing the boy for about five months in 2025.

Jessica Nakkan (left), who is represented by solicitor Himangi Ticku, will face court to be sentenced in 2027. Photo: Albert McKnight.

But the prosecutor also said the parties had not yet agreed to the facts of the case and would do so within a week.

This means the particular details of the crime Nakkan admitted to are not yet known.

Justice Jon White SC ordered a pre-sentence report and an assessment for an intensive corrections order.

He continued Nakkan’s bail and adjourned for sentencing to begin on 6 April 2027.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

australia.title: Family and sexual violence rates against Australian children rise sharply as researchers warn of ‘manosphere’
australia.snippet: Study authors say increase cannot be attributed to any one factor and list income inequality and growing awareness as other likely reason...
australia.content:
The sexual assault of Australian children has accelerated sharply since the pandemic, surprising researchers who expected rates to have fallen but instead found attacks on boys had risen 15.7%.

Researchers expected rates to have dropped in line with other countries around the world and warn the troubling findings show an urgent need to prevent the suffering of children.

The University of Sydney research published on Wednesday found a significant increase in violence against children between 2014 and 2024 that could be attributed to a range of factors, including income inequality and the manosphere.

An increase in reporting due to growing awareness could also partially explain the higher rate of violence, it found.

The study found a steady increase in rates of sexual assaults against girls aged up to nine (2.8% per year) and aged 10 to 17 (4.2%), with rates among boys aged 10 to 17 accelerating sharply after 2021 (15.7%).

Family violence-related assault showed a similar trend, with stable to modest increases before 2021 followed by steep increases thereafter.

Assault-related hospitalisations and child maltreatment were generally stable.

“In Australia, income inequality is at its highest point in 20 years, with substantial increases from 2021, coinciding with the acceleration of rates found in the current study,” researchers found.

“Economic stress may be especially salient in the post-2020 period, when pandemic-related financial disruptions intensified for many families, while government benefits providing economic relief, such as the JobKeeper payment scheme in Australia, ended in March 2021.

“Shifts in gender norms and online cultures may also play a role … traditional gender attitudes that favor male authority within households are resurging among young men [and] the expansion of misogynistic online communities and broader toxic masculinity narratives are associated with hostility toward women and girls.”

The research, published in the media journal JAMA Network Open, was based on an analysis of a decades-worth of Australian data from multiple sources.

These sources included national police-recorded assaults, hospitalisations, and child protection data from three Australian national agency databases.

The study’s lead author, Dr Lucy Grummitt, said researchers expected to find that the rate of violence against children had fallen, given evidence recorded in other high-income countries over the past decade regarding child protection.

That they found the opposite was impossible to attribute to any one factor, she said, but it did show the need for a less siloed approach to the issue.

“All these different departments that are involved in the bigger picture of violence against children are just focused on one particular subset, and we don’t actually have a very clear picture of what young people are being exposed to, and how has that changed over the last decade,” Grummitt said.

“So that was kind of the rationale … I expected to see that things were kind of improving, I suppose. But that’s not really what we found.

“Violence against children is a human rights issue, it shouldn’t be falling to one government department to be monitoring this … it really is a whole-of-government issue and currently our data and our monitoring really doesn’t reflect that.”

Grummitt said that it was frustrating for researchers to discover that in some cases entire datasets they hoped to use in the triangulation were missing.

This data included one year of missing child maltreatment data for NSW and Queensland, and family violence-related assault data for Queensland, Victoria, and Western Australia also being incomplete.

The data that did exist was also not directly comparable across states, Grummitt said.

“Family domestic violence data is improving, but it’s pretty striking that in 2024 when we finished extracting the data that there weren’t already these nationally consistent definitions.”

australia.title: AFL tells Sportsbet to stop using players in AI generated content
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Gambling firm working with AFL ‘on the evolving use of AI in our content’ as it deletes video depicting Lachie Neale saying ‘I...
australia.content:
The AFL has told its official gambling partner, Sportsbet, to stop featuring its high-profile athletes in AI-generated social media content without their permission.

Sportsbet has also been told to delete AI videos depicting AFL stars delivering lines from movies, television shows or speeches to react to real events.

The videos were age-restricted and designed to boost Sportsbet’s engagement on social media, in a bid for new audiences and customers.

The videos were published despite the federal government legislating to ban athletes appearing in gambling ads. The new rules take effect next year.

One recent AI video depicts former Brisbane Lions premiership player Lachie Neale accepting an award at his new club, Collingwood. Sportsbet manipulated his image to show him mimicking a 2018 speech from the US rapper Snoop Dogg accepting a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

“Last but not least, I want to thank me,” an AI-generated video of Neale said. “I want to thank me for believing in me. I want to thank me for doing all this hard work.”

Another AI-generated video depicts the Brisbane Lions player Will Ashcroft. The dual Norm Smith medallist was shown screaming a line from the television show Ozark: “If you want to stop me you’re going to have to fucking kill me”.

Sportsbet suggested this was Ashcroft’s response to Fremantle playing Wharfie Time in the final quarter of the 2026 AFL grand final.

The videos were removed from its Instagram page on Tuesday afternoon, after Sportsbet was contacted by Guardian Australia.

The gambling company has also created AI content using the images of the Hawthorn coach, Sam Mitchell, and former North Melbourne coach Alastair Clarkson.

While these videos were designed to be humorous, the AFL Players’ Association (AFLPA) said it was not impressed.

The AFLPA, which acts as a union, wrote to the league late last week with its concerns. It argued the videos breached a collective bargaining agreement between players and the AFL, which restricts how their images can be used by the league’s partners.

The association’s general manager of legal affairs, Alex Taverner, said: “AI generated player imagery is not permitted without the players’ approval.”

“We raised this with the AFL and advocated for both the removal of the content and a cessation of the use of AI-generated imagery and vision of players without their approval.

“Importantly, the AFL will now work with Sportsbet to remove the content.”

An AFL spokesperson said it would “continue to work closely with our partners on the use of AI content and will continue to do so as the technology evolves”.

A Sportsbet spokesperson said the company is “always developing content that entertains fans and supports engagement with sport”.

“We listen to our partners’ feedback and respond accordingly,” the spokesperson said.

“We’re continuing to work with the AFL on the evolving use of AI in our content, taking account of partner feedback and community expectations.”

The 2023-2027 collective bargaining agreement allows Sportsbet to use images and vision of players without permission, but only in certain circumstances and with restrictions. The agreement makes no mention of AI.

Independent ACT senator, David Pocock, a former professional athlete who focuses on the gambling industry and AI, said the case highlighted a need for tougher regulation.

“AI being used to generate images of elite athletes without their consent to promote harmful gambling products and attempt to buy social licensce exposes issues with gambling company behaviour as well as the lack of safeguards against deep fakes,” Pocock said.

Dr Mark Johnson, a senior lecturer at the University of Sydney who has researched social media influencers and gambling, said Sportsbet could have taken more care.

“The most likely explanation is that someone at Sportsbet acted without thinking and never paused to consider how the images of sportspeople are, themselves, often an element of brands and ownership,” Johnson said.

australia.title: Flying foxes in NSW and Victoria face mass starvation amid food shortages
australia.snippet: Rescuers respond to surge in callouts for the vulnerable bat species, which usually feeds on blossoms and tree nectar Get our breaking ne...
australia.content:
Flying foxes are starving en masse across New South Wales and parts of Victoria, with wildlife rescuers responding to a surge in reports of “exhausted and emaciated” adults and skeletal pups.

Most reports involved grey-headed flying foxes, listed as vulnerable under federal environment laws and which usually feed on the blossoms and nectar of native trees.

They are now facing food shortages across NSW, from the northern rivers to the south coast, according to the state’s environment department. Rescue organisations in Victoria are also experiencing an uptick in callouts, particularly in East Gippsland and Castlemaine.

Rachael Smethurst, the bat coordinator at Fawna wildlife rescue on the NSW mid-north coast, said the organisation was receiving 50 to 90 calls each day – more than the total number of callouts for bats in the previous nine months.

The bats were starving, she said. “They’re coming into back yards to eat ornamental fruit trees and eating a lot of ripe and unripe cocos palms. They’re crawling around on the ground eating unripe dropped fruit, and quite literally dropping out of trees due to starvation.”

Flying foxes were staying in back yards because they lacked the energy to fly back to camp, she said. Many were already dead, including pups that had been born prematurely.

Wildlife rescue organisation Wires said the mass starvation event was likely the result of habitat loss and a dry winter, with poor seasonal flowering of eucalypts and other natives.

“Many malnourished and dehydrated female flying foxes are in the final month of their gestational period and are tragically losing their young. They just haven’t got the nutritional health or strength to produce milk or carry to full term,” the organisation said.

Some animals were displaying unusual behaviour as they struggled to find food and water. “They’re eating off the ground, drinking water from the grass after the rain, and hanging too low in trees.”

Wires wildlife vet Dr Vere Nicolson said caring for premature pups was “labour intensive and not universally successful”, with the response made more challenging due to the number of animals involved.

Tamsyn Hogarth, director of the Fly By Night Bat Clinic, said rescuers in Victoria were seeing many “exhausted and emaciated” bats and starving babies “like little skeletons”, which appeared to be coming from NSW.

Bats spending time in people’s back yards during the day was a red flag, she said. “They’re so hungry they’re actually eating during the day, away from the safety of the camp,” she said. There were a lot of dead pups under trees, and incidents with barbed wire, dog attacks and electrocution had also increased.

“We don’t know for sure what is causing this particular incident, but food shortages can be aggravated by climatic events such as drought and El Niño conditions,” a NSW environment department spokesperson said.

The state’s health department reminded the community to avoid touching or handling bats, after 43 people were assessed having been scratched or bitten in the past two weeks.

People were encouraged to report sick or dead bats to their local wildlife rescue, Hogarth said. That enabled volunteers to check for pups, rehabilitate animals where possible, and help ease the suffering of others – although access to veterinarians able to provide euthanasia was challenging, with so many reports coming from regional or rural areas.

Hogarth said grey-headed flying foxes usually gave birth to one young per year, so the loss of so many pups would have a “terrible ripple effect” for the species. The food shortages followed thousands of heat deaths this summer, and came amid disruptions to Melbourne’s Yarra Bend camp from freeway construction works. “They’re copping it everywhere, they can’t catch a break.”

australia.title: The RBA keeps hiking interest rates – but are the rate rises actually working?
australia.snippet: With the cash rate at a 15-year high, consumer confidence has tanked – while household spending is still growing Get our breaking news em...
australia.content:
Interest rates have risen to 15-year highs and are pushing up mortgage default risks – but household spending is still growing.

Economists say the surprising result shows this year’s four rate hikes have not yet fully hit the economy and may be less effective at fighting inflation than they used to be. If true, that could mean more interest rate rises are on the way.

What is the RBA trying to achieve by increasing interest rates?

The Reserve Bank has increased its key cash rate to cut household spending and discourage businesses and workers from seeking higher prices and wages. It aims to bring inflation back under 3%.

Financial institutions now face higher funding costs and have responded by lifting the rates they charge for home loans, business loans or bonds for big companies.

But eight months on from the year’s first rate rise in February, spending is not going backwards.

Economic activity has slowed, businesses are less efficient and real wages are going backwards compared with a year ago as inflation rises. But Australian household spending has accelerated, up nearly 7% compared with a year ago, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics estimates.

Part of the increase in spending is from higher prices for essentials such as fuel and food. But it also reflects strong demand for electric cars and non-essentials – particularly overseas travel.

Inflation has risen to 4% as of August, both because of oil disruption and mass construction of big projects like datacentres and because local businesses are lifting their prices. When customers are willing to spend big, businesses find it easier to raise prices.

Do higher mortgage rates cut household budgets?

The cash rate’s most immediate effect is on household cashflow, taking money away from borrowers while giving more to debt-free savers.

RBA data shows higher rates and prices have left 2% of borrowers unable to afford essential expenses but most people are meeting repayments.

Warren Hogan, the managing director of EQ Economics, says the emergence of mortgage offset accounts in the last decade has reduced rates’ effect on cashflow. Borrowers who have spare cash in offset accounts, often because they can afford to pay more than their minimum, now have “massive buffers”. Australians now hold nearly $350bn in total in offset balances.

“You just didn’t have the same amount of capacity to pay off earlier and have offsets accounts and all that sort of thing,” Hogan says.

Home ownership is in decline, meaning more Australians are renters whose spending is not directly hit by higher mortgage rates.

One in three households own their home debt-free and benefit from higher interest on their savings. Commonwealth Bank data indicates older Australians and debt-free homeowners have steadily increased their spending this year.

Will falling house prices discourage spending?

The slide in house prices is a sign that interest rates and higher borrowing costs are directly restricting economic activity, according to David Bassanese, the chief economist at BetaShares.

House price slides are also an indirect channel for hikes to slow spending as homeowners tend to cut back when falls in home values make them less wealthy than they had been. RBA research suggests a 10% fall in housing prices – which is expected by mid-2027 – will cut consumption by 1.5%.

Bassanese says consumer spending does not appear to have slowed yet by as much as past RBA models would imply. “We’re probably not seeing a major effect yet, but in theory, it should be starting to happen,” he said.

The “wealth effect” of interest rates is typically slower-moving than the cashflow effect.

But most homeowners are also wealthier than they were two years ago, with the median national price back to where it was in September.

What about exchange rates?

The Reserve Bank says the most important effect of interest rate rises is through the exchange rate. Higher interest rates tend to push up demand to invest in Australia, lifting the Australian dollar, making imports cheaper.

But the dollar has been fairly stable against other currencies because foreign central banks like the US Federal Reserve are also lifting their own interest rates.

The Australian dollar rose from 65 US cents in November 2025 to 72 in May 2026, after the first three RBA rate rises but has fallen to 69 US cents. It’s followed a similar path compared to an index of Australia’s trade partners, include China, Japan, Europe and South Korea.

“We’re raising rates, but so is everybody else,” Bassanese says. “Our currency is not especially strong, although it has lifted somewhat over the past year.”

How does higher unemployment stop inflation?

Interest rate rises aim to push up unemployment but the hikes have had little effect this year.

More jobseekers make it easier for businesses to find workers without lifting wages. Higher wages would be passed on as higher prices for customers so more unemployment tends to mean less inflation.

But the jobs market has been surprisingly strong. Health and care sectors have rapidly hired thanks to bigger demand and government subsidies while productivity is going backwards, forcing businesses to hire more workers to keep up production.

The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, has said she wants to see a small increase in jobless rates so there is less pressure from wages on prices, drawing criticism from unions.

Unemployment increasing from 4.6% to 5% would represent an extra 60,000 people out of work if the workforce stayed the same size.

But Bullock said after September’s rate hike that she does not expect job losses, instead hoping job creation will slow and more people will look to join the workforce, leaving jobseekers searching for longer periods.

Markets expect only one more rate rise and not until May 2027. But the Deutsche Bank strategist Lachlan Dynan warns rate rises’ weaker effects add to the risk of another hike.

“The Australian household sector has been more resilient to hikes than many expected,” Dynan says. “Risks to RBA [rates] are back to being skewed to the upside in our view.”

australia.title: How Firmus went from Australia’s AI 'fairytale' to flop - podcast
australia.snippet: It was supposed to be an Australian business success story. Just over a week ago local AI company Firmus was preparing to hit the market ...
australia.content:
It was supposed to be an Australian business success story. Just over a week ago local AI company Firmus was preparing to hit the market with a value that would put the startup in the same league as Woolworths. But last Friday, everything fell apart.

At the centre was Firmus co-founder Oliver Curtis, an entrepreneur trying to rebuild his reputation after spending time in prison for insider trading. Curtis said the collapse was down to Australia’s ‘mantra of disbelief around entrepreneurs’.

Business editor Jonathan Barrett speaks to Matilda Boseley about the hubris of the firm’s founders and what this says about the future of the AI investment bubble

world.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
world.snippet: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers A controversial research trial ...
world.content:
A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.

It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.

Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.

Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.

The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.

The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.

The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.

In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.

Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.

According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.

The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.

“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.

Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.

The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.

Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.

This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”

When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.

Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

world.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
world.snippet: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza The Nobel peace...
world.content:
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.

Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.

“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”

In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.

“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.

“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”

Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.

The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.

Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.

The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.

The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.

“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.

Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa, home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.

“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.

Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.

“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.

In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.

“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.

Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.

On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

world.title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
world.snippet: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the f...
world.content:
Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.

The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.

In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.

Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.

The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.

In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

world.title: Egyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleagues
world.snippet: Matsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim Brotherhood Egyptian journalists...
world.content:
Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.

Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.

One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.

“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.

In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.

Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.

Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.

Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.

The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.

For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.

“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”

world.title: Scientists discover 180,000 giant tortoises on one Seychelles island
world.snippet: Free-roaming Aldabra population far exceeds human population of Seychelles after decades-long recovery programme A survey of the world’s ...
world.content:
A survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has discovered that the once endangered species is thriving.

A population of Aldabra giant tortoises lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.

The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island. This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.

The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022. It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.

Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.

Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, the CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.

In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island, but a recovery programme led to it becoming a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.

Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.

“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”

Despite the good news, the study’s authors say that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.

The study authors say invasive mammals remain a threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.

“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.

“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.

“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”
